units.title: Unit 41 — Describing objects
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 41. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish common opposing adjectives for materials, colours, appearance and durability.
Use adjective, noun and verb families accurately when evaluating objects or designs.
Make natural comparisons and degrees of description with informal intensifiers.
Recognise figurative uses such as a genuine smile, a stiff manner and solid work.

items.example: The tabletop is made from natural stone.
items.note: Not made artificially; contrast with artificial.

items.example: The flowers look real, but they are artificial.
items.note: Made by people rather than occurring naturally.

items.example: The artist used vivid shades of blue and orange.
items.note: Bright, striking and clear, especially of colours or descriptions.

items.example: The reception area was decorated in sombre grey.
items.note: Dark or serious in appearance; British spelling is sombre.

items.example: We chose a conventional rectangular desk.
items.note: Following familiar and widely accepted designs or methods.

items.example: The museum displayed a bizarre chair shaped like a hand.
items.note: Very unusual or strange, often surprisingly so.

items.example: The container has a transparent lid.
items.note: Allows light through so objects behind it can be seen.

items.example: The opaque screen hides the equipment behind it.
items.note: Does not allow you to see through it.

items.example: The second prototype was perfect in every detail.
items.note: Having no faults; compare a perfect machine with a faulty one.

items.example: A faulty switch prevented the motor from starting.
items.note: Not working as it should because of a defect.

items.example: This cable is too stiff to bend around the corner.
items.note: Hard to bend or move; it can also describe tense behaviour.

items.example: The flexible hose fits into narrow spaces.
items.note: Able to bend without breaking; also adaptable to changes.

items.example: Wash this delicate fabric by hand.
items.note: Easily damaged and needing careful treatment.

items.example: The protective case is made from tough plastic.
items.note: Difficult to damage; also means difficult in other contexts.

items.example: Put a fragile label on the glass package.
items.note: Easily broken, particularly by impact.

items.example: A sturdy shelf can hold all these reference books.
items.note: Strongly made and unlikely to break or fall.

items.example: I prefer strong coffee without much milk.
items.note: Strong refers to an intense flavour, not physical strength.

items.example: This coffee tastes weak because there is too much water.
items.note: Weak refers to a mild or diluted flavour.

items.example: The dealer confirmed that the watch was genuine.
items.note: Authentic and not a copy; can also describe sincere feelings.

items.example: The signature was fake, not the artist’s original work.
items.note: Not real or authentic; can function as an adjective or noun.

items.example: A plain wooden frame suited the photograph.
items.note: Without decorative details; not necessarily unattractive.

items.example: The hall has decorative tiles around the doorway.
items.note: Intended to make something look attractive.

items.example: We need a decent-sized table for the meeting.
items.note: Of an acceptable or reasonably good standard; often used in decent size.

items.example: He had the decency to apologise for arriving late.
items.note: Acceptable, respectful behaviour; commonly have the decency to do something.

items.example: They spent the entire afternoon fixing the equipment.
items.note: All of something, with no part excluded.

items.example: Please read the document in its entirety.
items.note: The whole of something; in its entirety is a common formal phrase.

items.example: Wide windows are characteristic of older factories.
items.note: Adjective usually followed by of when linking a typical feature to a group.

items.example: Reliability is a key characteristic of this design.
items.note: Countable noun meaning a typical or distinguishing feature.

items.example: The building has a distinctive character.
items.note: The distinctive nature or qualities of someone or something.

items.example: Compact dimensions characterise this product range.
items.note: Verb related to characteristic; British spelling is characterise.

items.example: The technician recorded the precise position of the shaft.
items.note: Exact and carefully specified; a precise measurement.

items.example: The task requires a high degree of precision.
items.note: Accuracy and exactness, particularly for measurements.

items.example: The office has a severe design with bare concrete walls.
items.note: Here: plain, strict or stark in appearance; elsewhere: very serious.

items.example: The inspector assessed the severity of the damage.
items.note: Degree of seriousness or harshness.

items.example: The shelves are made of solid oak rather than veneer.
items.note: Made of one material all the way through; figuratively reliable or good.

items.example: We appreciated the solidity of the new desk.
items.note: The quality of being firm, strong or solid.

items.example: The liquid will solidify as it cools.
items.note: Become solid or make something more definite or firm.

items.example: The mistake may look trivial, but we should fix it.
items.note: Not important or serious; contrasted with significant.

items.example: They disagreed over a triviality and missed the main issue.
items.note: A very minor detail or the quality of being unimportant.

items.example: The podcast includes interesting science trivia.
items.note: Small facts, often entertaining but not very important.

items.example: We should not trivialise concerns about workplace safety.
items.note: Make an important matter seem less serious than it is.

items.example: A great big dog was sleeping beside the door.
items.note: Informal spoken intensifier; great big emphasises physical size.

items.pt: nem de longe tão interessante quanto
items.example: The remake is not half as interesting as the original film.
items.note: A conversational comparison meaning much less interesting.

items.pt: nem de longe tão caro quanto
items.example: This monitor is nowhere near as expensive as that model.
items.note: A strong negative comparison; nowhere near as + adjective + as.

items.pt: excepcionalmente; mais do que o habitual
items.example: The library was unusually quiet this morning.
items.note: More than is normal or expected.

items.example: The replacement part is reasonably cheap.
items.note: Fairly or moderately; often suggests a satisfactory degree.

items.example: The final prototype looks pretty good to me.
items.note: Informal pretty + adjective means fairly or quite; not about attractiveness.

items.example: This handbook is pretty thick for an introductory guide.
items.note: Pretty is an informal degree adverb here.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: His proposal was creative, but it was not frivolous.
items.note: Not serious or sensible; contrasted with severe in the exercise.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: She gave the visitors a genuine smile.
items.note: Genuine can refer to sincere emotions, not just authentic objects.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The lecturer presented a transparent argument with clear evidence.
items.note: Figurative transparent means easy to understand or see through logically.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The journalist described the scene vividly.
items.note: Vividly means in a clear, lively way that creates a mental picture.

items.pt: maneira rígida; comportamento pouco à vontade
items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: He spoke in a stiff manner during the formal introduction.
items.note: Figurative stiff can mean tense, formal or unnatural in behaviour.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The teacher said the essay was solid work.
items.note: Figurative solid describes something dependable or of a good standard.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The fragile china cups were packed separately.
items.note: As a common noun, china means porcelain, not the country.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The leggings contain Lycra to make them stretch.
items.note: A trademark used for elastic synthetic fibres.

items.section: D · Exercise vocabulary and extended uses
items.example: The gallery confirmed that it was a genuine painting.
items.note: The adjective genuine can modify artworks whose authenticity matters.

units.title: Unit 42 — Belief and opinion
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 42. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Express degrees of certainty and opinion through verbs with appropriate register.
Use in my view, to my mind and from my point of view with their correct prepositions.
Describe beliefs, ideologies, convictions and philosophies with neutral vocabulary.
Distinguish intensity, unconventionality and moderation in adjectives describing opinions.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: I am convinced that the measurements are correct.
items.note: Be convinced that expresses a very strong feeling of certainty.

items.pt: sustentar que; defender a opinião de que
items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: Some researchers hold that more testing is necessary.
items.note: Formal verb of firmly held belief; typically hold that + clause.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: She maintains that the original estimate was accurate.
items.note: Formal: continue insisting a claim is true, even when challenged.

items.pt: achar que; ter a opinião de que
items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: I feel that the team needs more time to prepare.
items.note: Expresses a personal, often strongly felt opinion.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: I reckon the meeting will finish before lunch.
items.note: Informal, especially British English; used for a prediction or judgement.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: I doubt that the replacement will arrive today.
items.note: Expresses disbelief or uncertainty; the b is silent.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: I suspect that the figures are incomplete.
items.note: Have a feeling something is true, often an unwelcome fact.

items.section: A · Verbs of belief and opinion
items.example: He was convinced that he had seen the device before.
items.note: Be convinced may be followed by a that-clause or of + noun.

items.pt: na minha opinião; a meu ver
items.example: In my view, we should repeat the experiment.
items.note: Fairly formal expression; say in my view, not to my view.

items.example: In my opinion, the second solution is safer.
items.note: General opinion marker: always in, not on my opinion.

items.example: To my mind, the report needs a clearer conclusion.
items.note: Fairly informal in this unit; use to, not in my mind.

items.example: If you ask me, this deadline is unrealistic.
items.note: Informal opinion expression; no actual question is required.

items.example: From my point of view, the plan is too expensive.
items.note: Use from, not in my point of view.

items.word: from a teacher’s point of view
items.pt: do ponto de vista de um professor
items.example: From a teacher’s point of view, smaller classes may be better.
items.note: Can describe how a situation affects a particular person or group.

items.example: Many people believe in life after death.
items.note: Believe in + person, idea or existence; believe that + clause is different.

items.example: We asked residents for their views on the new bridge.
items.note: Plural views on + topic; opinion on/about is also possible.

items.pt: achar de; ter uma opinião sobre
items.example: What do you think of the new supervisor?
items.note: Think of asks for a judgement or opinion about someone or something.

items.example: Are you for changing the timetable?
items.note: Informal or neutral stance marker; contrasted with against.

items.example: Several residents are against the proposal.
items.note: Expresses opposition; often used with be against + noun or -ing.

items.example: Most of the committee are in favour of the changes.
items.note: Followed by a noun or -ing form; British spelling is favour.

items.example: I am opposed to cancelling the training session.
items.note: Adjective + to + noun or -ing form; fairly formal in this context.

items.example: We have doubts about the reliability of that result.
items.note: Use doubts about + noun or -ing; often signals reservation.

items.example: She has strong views on public transport.
items.note: The adjective strong modifies the noun views; follow with on.

items.example: The decision reflected his personal beliefs.
items.note: An idea accepted as true; plural beliefs is common.

items.example: The essay compares two political ideologies.
items.note: An organised set of political or social beliefs.

items.example: She defended her position with conviction.
items.note: A firmly held belief; not only the legal meaning of conviction.

items.example: His teaching philosophy encourages independent thinking.
items.note: A systematic approach to life or ideas, or the academic discipline.

items.example: The debate featured several left-wing speakers.
items.note: A political descriptor; meaning depends on national context.

items.example: A right-wing candidate joined the discussion.
items.note: A political descriptor; meaning depends on national context.

items.example: The political scientist described the movement as socialist.
items.note: A person or idea associated with socialism.

items.example: The newspaper described the policy as conservative.
items.note: Can describe a political position or resistance to change.

items.example: The historian discussed a Darwinist interpretation of evolution.
items.note: A person influenced by the evolutionary ideas associated with Darwin.

items.example: The speaker has been vegetarian for ten years.
items.note: Someone who does not eat meat or fish; may also modify food.

items.example: The peace campaign attracted many pacifists.
items.note: Someone who opposes war and violence as a way of resolving disputes.

items.example: A Muslim colleague explained the tradition to the group.
items.note: A follower of Islam; as an adjective, Muslim also refers to this religion.

items.example: The survey included questions about religious beliefs.
items.note: Beliefs connected with religion; a neutral category, not one ideology.

items.example: Her moral convictions influenced how she made decisions.
items.note: Firm beliefs about right and wrong.

items.example: Employees may have different personal convictions.
items.note: Strong individual beliefs, which can differ from group ideologies.

items.example: Their intellectual beliefs shaped the academic debate.
items.note: Ideas held on philosophical, academic or theoretical grounds.

items.example: A fanatical supporter travelled to every match.
items.note: Extremely enthusiastic or devoted; can suggest excessive intensity.

items.example: His obsessive attention to minor details delayed the project.
items.note: An excessive and persistent preoccupation with something.

items.example: The inventor became known for his eccentric ideas.
items.note: Unconventional in an unusual, sometimes amusing way.

items.example: That is an odd suggestion for a safety procedure.
items.note: Strange or unexpected; often milder than weird.

items.example: The witness described a weird sequence of events.
items.note: Informal, often stronger than odd or more unsettling.

items.example: The college follows a traditional teaching approach.
items.note: Following established customs or methods.

items.example: She supports a middle-of-the-road political platform.
items.note: Neither very left-wing nor very right-wing; often about politics.

items.example: He expressed a moderate position during the debate.
items.note: Not extreme; may concern politics, beliefs or the degree of something.

items.example: She is a dedicated volunteer at the community centre.
items.note: Devoting a lot of effort and time to a cause, activity or person.

items.example: He is committed to improving educational access.
items.note: Strongly devoted to a belief or goal; often committed to + noun/-ing.

items.example: She has a firm belief in equal opportunities.
items.note: Firm describes a belief held confidently and not easily changed.

items.example: He expressed a strong belief in the value of education.
items.note: Strong emphasises how deeply a belief is held.

items.example: The committee considered a radical reform proposal.
items.note: In favour of fundamental or far-reaching change; context matters.

items.example: The proposal was criticised as too extreme.
items.note: Very far from what is typical or moderate; often evaluative.

items.example: She described her views as moderate and liberal.
items.note: Political meaning varies by country; can also describe openness to change.

items.example: The lecturer outlined a Marxist interpretation of the economy.
items.note: A person or idea associated with Marxist political and economic theory.

items.pt: defensor convicto; pessoa que acredita firmemente
items.example: Maya is a firm believer in lifelong learning.
items.note: Firm believer in + noun or -ing expresses strong commitment.

items.example: The team has a few fanatical supporters who attend every game.
items.note: An intensive adjective + noun combination.

items.example: He did not want to sound like a moralist when giving advice.
items.note: Someone strongly concerned with morality or judging behaviour.

items.example: She is an intellectual who enjoys debating new ideas.
items.note: Here a countable noun for someone interested in serious ideas.

items.example: A traditionalist might prefer older methods of teaching.
items.note: Someone who strongly values established customs or practices.

items.example: The philosopher challenged assumptions about knowledge.
items.note: A person who studies or develops ideas about existence and reasoning.

items.example: The reformer was described as a radical thinker.
items.note: Someone whose ideas challenge accepted assumptions.

items.example: A manager should not impose personal views on the whole team.
items.note: Verb pattern: impose something on somebody.

items.example: I doubt that this plan will solve every problem.
items.note: The book practises transforming a suspicion into doubt that + clause.

items.example: The evidence convinced the reviewers that the method was reliable.
items.note: Convince someone that + clause is transitive; be convinced describes the result.

items.example: He is suspicious of change even when it could help.
items.note: Suspicious of + noun or person; related in meaning to a conservative view.

items.example: Calling every small delay a disaster seems absurd.
items.note: Extremely unreasonable or illogical; used in the opinion exercise.

items.pt: nem de esquerda nem de direita
items.example: The candidate presents herself as neither left nor right.
items.note: A neutral way of explaining a middle-of-the-road political stance.
